grief_counselor.title: Grief Counselors & Therapists
grief_counselor.description: Mental health professionals who specialize in helping people process loss and grief.
whenToSeek: You're struggling to function in daily life
Grief feels overwhelming or isn't easing over time
You want professional support processing your loss
You're experiencing complicated emotions (guilt, anger, relief)
You want a safe space to talk without burdening family

whatToLookFor.why: General therapists may not understand the unique aspects of grief. Look for someone with specific training or certification in grief counseling.

whatToLookFor.criteria: Licensed credentials (LCSW, LPC, LMFT, PhD, PsyD)
whatToLookFor.why: Licensure ensures they've met education and training requirements. Common credentials include Licensed Clinical Social Worker (LCSW), Licensed Professional Counselor (LPC), or psychologist.

whatToLookFor.criteria: Experience with your type of loss
whatToLookFor.why: Losing a parent has unique dynamics. Someone who has worked with adult children grieving parents will understand your experience better.
Some people prefer structured approaches, others want open-ended talk therapy. Ask about their style before committing.
Therapy only helps if you can actually attend. Consider whether they take your insurance, offer sliding scale fees, or provide online sessions.

redFlags: Promises to 'fix' your grief quickly
Pushes religious or spiritual frameworks without your consent
Makes you feel judged for how you're grieving
Doesn't have proper licensure
Won't discuss their approach or credentials
questionsToAsk: What is your experience working with grief and loss?
What's your approach to grief counseling?
Do you have experience with adult children who have lost parents?
What are your fees and do you take insurance?
Do you offer telehealth sessions?
How long do clients typically work with you?

costRange.notes: Many therapists offer sliding scale fees. Some insurance plans cover grief counseling. Community mental health centers may offer lower-cost options.

estate_attorney.title: Estate & Probate Attorneys
estate_attorney.description: Lawyers who specialize in probate, estate administration, and related legal matters.
whenToSeek: The estate needs to go through probate
There's a will that needs to be validated
There are disputes among heirs or beneficiaries
The estate includes complex assets (businesses, multiple properties)
You're unsure about your legal responsibilities as executor
There are potential creditor claims or lawsuits

whatToLookFor.criteria: Specialization in probate and estate administration
whatToLookFor.why: Probate law is complex and varies by state. You want someone who does this regularly, not a general practitioner handling their first estate.
Probate laws vary significantly by state. An attorney licensed and experienced in your state will know local court procedures and requirements.
Estate attorneys may charge hourly, flat fees, or a percentage of the estate. Understand the total cost before engaging.
You'll have many questions during this process. Choose someone who explains things clearly and responds promptly.
For simple estates, a solo practitioner may be fine. For complex estates, a larger firm may have more resources.

redFlags: Unwilling to provide a fee estimate
Pressures you to make quick decisions
Doesn't explain your options clearly
Takes on work outside their expertise
Poor reviews regarding communication
questionsToAsk: What percentage of your practice is probate and estate work?
How do you charge for your services?
Can you give me an estimate of total costs for my situation?
How long does the probate process typically take in this county?
Who will be my main point of contact?
How quickly do you typically respond to questions?

costRange.notes: Costs vary widely based on estate complexity. Some attorneys charge 2-4% of the estate value. Simple estates with no disputes cost less.

estate_cpa.title: CPAs & Tax Professionals
estate_cpa.description: Accountants who specialize in estate taxes, final tax returns, and estate accounting.
whenToSeek: You need to file the deceased's final tax return
The estate may owe estate taxes (estates over $12.92M in 2023)
There are complex assets requiring valuation
You need to understand the tax implications of inheritance
The estate has ongoing income (rental properties, businesses)
You want to ensure proper estate accounting

whatToLookFor.criteria: Experience with estate and trust taxation
whatToLookFor.why: Estate tax rules are specialized. A CPA who primarily does personal or business taxes may miss important considerations.
Certified Public Accountants (CPAs) and Enrolled Agents (EAs) have demonstrated expertise and are authorized to represent you before the IRS.
The best estate CPAs understand how taxes interact with probate, beneficiary designations, and estate distribution.
A good CPA will help you make decisions that minimize tax liability, not just file returns after the fact.

redFlags: No experience with estate or fiduciary returns
Unable to explain tax concepts clearly
Doesn't ask questions about the full situation
Promises specific outcomes before reviewing details
No clear engagement letter or fee agreement
questionsToAsk: How many estate returns have you prepared?
Are you familiar with the estate tax rules in my state?
What information will you need from me?
What is your fee structure?
Can you help with the deceased's final personal tax return as well?
What's your timeline for completing the work?

costRange.notes: Simple final returns cost less. Complex estates with estate tax returns cost more. Many estates don't owe federal estate tax due to the high exemption.

estate_sale.title: Estate Sale Companies
estate_sale.description: Professionals who organize, price, and sell household contents, typically taking a percentage of sales.
whenToSeek: There's significant household contents to sell
You don't have time to sell items individually
You're not sure what items are worth
The home needs to be cleared for sale or end of lease
There are antiques or collectibles requiring expertise

whatToLookFor.why: Estate sales involve trusting someone with your family's possessions. Look for companies with verifiable track records.
Most estate sale companies take 25-50% of gross sales. Understand exactly what's included in their fee.
Good companies can identify valuable items that might otherwise be underpriced. They should know antiques, collectibles, and current market values.
Understand who's responsible for unsold items, cleanup, and any additional fees. Get everything in writing.
Reputable companies carry liability insurance and may be bonded to protect against theft or damage.

redFlags: No written contract
Unwilling to provide references
Unusually high or low commission rates without explanation
Pressure to decide immediately
No clear plan for unsold items
No insurance or bonding
questionsToAsk: What is your commission rate and what does it include?
Can you provide references from recent sales?
How do you research and price items?
What happens to unsold items?
Do you carry insurance?
How long does the process take from start to finish?
Will you handle advertising and day-of staffing?

costRange.notes: Commission varies based on location, estate size, and value of contents. Some companies charge minimum fees for smaller estates.

donation_pickup.title: Donation Pickup Services
donation_pickup.description: Organizations that collect usable items from your home and donate them to those in need.
whenToSeek: You have usable items that didn't sell or aren't worth selling
You want items to benefit others rather than go to waste
You need help with heavy items or large quantities
You want tax deductions for donated items

whatToLookFor.why: Only donations to qualified nonprofits are tax-deductible. Ask for documentation of their tax-exempt status.
Understand what items they accept, how far in advance to schedule, and whether they'll take everything or cherry-pick.
For tax purposes, you'll need documentation of your donation. Reputable organizations provide itemized receipts.
Different organizations serve different populations. Choose one whose mission resonates with you or would have mattered to your parent.

redFlags: Won't provide proof of nonprofit status
No donation receipts
Charges significant fees (legitimate services are usually free)
Vague about where items go
Pressure tactics or pushy scheduling
questionsToAsk: Are you a 501(c)(3) organization?
What items do you accept and not accept?
Will you take everything or just select items?
How far in advance do I need to schedule?
Will you provide a donation receipt?
Where do the donated items go?

costRange.notes: Most legitimate donation services are free. Some may charge for large furniture removal. You may get a tax deduction for fair market value of donated items.

junk_removal.title: Junk Removal Services
junk_removal.description: Companies that haul away unwanted items, debris, and trash from a property.
whenToSeek: There are items that can't be donated or sold
The property needs complete cleanout
There's debris or damaged items to remove
You don't have the physical ability to haul items yourself
You need the job done quickly

whatToLookFor.why: Reputable companies provide quotes before starting. Avoid those who won't give you a price until after loading.
Companies hauling waste need proper permits. Insurance protects you if workers are injured on your property.
Good companies recycle and donate what they can, rather than dumping everything in a landfill.
You're coordinating a lot. You need companies that show up when they say they will.

redFlags: Won't give a written estimate
Significantly lower prices than competitors (may add fees later)
No physical address or business license
Poor reviews about hidden fees or no-shows
Unmarked vehicles or unprofessional appearance
questionsToAsk: Can you give me a firm quote in writing?
Are you licensed and insured?
What happens to the items you remove?
Do you recycle or donate usable items?
How quickly can you schedule the job?
Is there anything you won't take?

costRange.notes: Pricing is usually based on volume (how much of their truck you fill). Full home cleanouts may require multiple loads or flat-rate pricing.
